study.title: Living among those who hate peace
study.intro: Psalm 120 opens the fifteen Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120-134), short songs sung by pilgrims traveling up to Jerusalem for the great feasts. Fittingly, the journey begins far from home. The singer is surrounded by liars and people who love conflict, and he cries to the LORD for rescue. The first step toward God's house is admitting that where you are is not where you belong.
study.context: The Songs of Ascents were likely sung as worshipers 'went up' to Jerusalem, a city set high in the hills, three times a year for Passover, Pentecost and the Feast of Tabernacles. Psalm 120 starts the collection with distance and distress: Meshech lay far to the north near the Black Sea and Kedar in the Arabian desert to the east, two names standing for hostile, faraway places. From there the songs climb step by step until they end in praise in the temple courts in Psalm 134.
study.peopleNote: No author is named. The speaker is an unnamed worshiper living among hostile neighbors. Meshech and Kedar are distant peoples used as symbols of a hostile home. God is never portrayed as a human figure in planned art.

verses.title: A cry that was answered
verses.heading: In my distress I cried to the LORD
verses.meaning: 'In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me.' The pilgrim songs begin not with a parade but with a prayer from a hard place. The singer remembers that when he was hemmed in and troubled, he called out and God responded. That memory becomes the fuel for the whole journey. Every step toward the house of God starts with the confidence that the LORD actually hears people in trouble and does not ignore them.
verses.contextTitle: The first step of the ascent
verses.context: This is the first of fifteen songs headed 'a song of ascents.' Jonah 2:2 uses almost the same words from inside the fish, and Psalm 18:6 recalls David crying out in distress and being heard from God's temple.
explore: Song of ascents
A title given to Psalms 120-134, probably songs sung while going up to Jerusalem for the yearly festivals.
Distress
A tight, pressing situation; the Hebrew pictures being squeezed into a narrow place with no room.
verses.reflect: Think of a time you cried out to God in distress. How does remembering His answer help you face today?
verses.alt: A lone traveler pausing at the start of a rocky road at dawn.

verses.title: Rescue from lying lips
verses.heading: Deliver my soul from deceit
verses.meaning: 'Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips and a deceitful tongue.' The danger here is not swords but words. Slander, gossip and lies can wound as deeply as any weapon, and the singer feels powerless against them. He asks God to rescue his whole self, his soul, from people who twist the truth. It is an honest prayer for anyone who has been misrepresented and cannot set the record straight alone.
verses.context: Scripture takes the damage of lying seriously. Proverbs 12:22 says lying lips are detestable to the LORD, and James 3:6 calls the tongue a fire that can set a whole life ablaze. Psalm 52 describes a tongue that plots destruction like a sharpened razor.
explore: Deceitful tongue
Speech meant to mislead or trap others, saying one thing while intending harm.
Soul
In Hebrew, the whole living person, including life, desires and inner self, not just a spiritual part.
verses.reflect: Have you been hurt by lies or gossip? What would it look like to hand that hurt to God instead of fighting back with words?
verses.alt: Two figures whispering behind a market stall while a third walks past unaware.

verses.title: A question for the liar
verses.heading: What will be added to you?
verses.meaning: 'What will He do to you, and what will be added to you, O deceitful tongue?' The singer turns and speaks directly to the lying tongue itself. It is a pointed question: do you really think you will get away with this? Lies may seem to win for a time, but God sees and will respond. The verse reminds us that deceit always carries a cost, and that God, not the liar, has the final word.
verses.context: The phrasing echoes an old oath formula, 'May God do so to you and more also' (1 Samuel 3:17). Galatians 6:7 teaches that a person reaps what he sows, and Proverbs 19:5 says a false witness will not go unpunished.
explore: Added to you
An idiom for what more will happen to someone, here meaning the consequences that pile up for a liar.
Oath formula
A traditional way of calling down consequences, used in Israel to stress how serious a matter was.
verses.reflect: Why is it freeing to trust that God will deal with lies instead of carrying the job of payback yourself?
verses.alt: A small oil lamp burning on a stone ledge in a dim room.

verses.title: Arrows and burning coals
verses.heading: Coals of the broom tree
verses.meaning: 'Sharp arrows will come from the warrior, with burning coals of the broom tree!' Here is the answer to the question. The lying tongue, which shot words like arrows, will meet God's sharper arrows. Broom tree wood was known in the desert for making charcoal that burned hot and long. The picture is fitting judgment: those who set others on fire with lies will face a fire of their own. God's justice matches the harm done.
verses.context: Lies are often compared to arrows in the Psalms (Psalm 64:3) and to fire (James 3:6). The broom tree, a desert shrub, is the bush Elijah rested under in 1 Kings 19:4. Its roots made charcoal valued for its lasting heat.
explore: Broom tree
A desert shrub with white flowers whose wood and roots made hot, long-burning charcoal.
Warrior
A trained fighter; here a picture of God acting decisively against those who harm with words.
verses.reflect: How does knowing that God sees and will answer injustice help you let go of the urge to get even?
verses.alt: A desert shrub with small white flowers beside a glowing campfire at dusk.

verses.title: Far from home
verses.heading: Among the tents of Kedar
verses.meaning: 'Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar!' The singer groans about where he lives. Meshech was far to the north and Kedar was a desert people to the southeast; no one could live in both at once. These are symbols, the way someone might say they live among barbarians. He feels like a foreigner surrounded by people who do not share his faith or values, and he aches for a different home.
verses.context: Meshech appears in Ezekiel 38:2 among warlike northern nations, and Kedar was a nomadic Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13). Hebrews 11:13 describes the faithful as strangers and exiles on earth longing for a better country.
explore: Meshech
A distant people in the far north near the Black Sea, remembered in Scripture as warlike.
Kedar
A nomadic desert tribe in Arabia who lived in dark goat-hair tents, descended from Ishmael.
verses.reflect: Where do you feel out of place because of your faith? How might that longing point you toward God?
verses.alt: Dark goat-hair tents pitched across a dry, windy plain.

verses.title: Weary of hostility
verses.heading: Too long among those who hate peace
verses.meaning: 'Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace.' The complaint grows tired and heavy. It is not one bad day but a long season of living around people who seem to thrive on conflict. Constant hostility wears down a person's spirit. The honesty of this verse gives us permission to tell God when we are exhausted by our surroundings and want something better.
verses.context: Psalm 55:6 longs for wings like a dove to fly away from strife. Romans 12:18 urges believers, as far as it depends on them, to live at peace with everyone, while knowing that peace is not always returned.
explore: Dwelt
Lived or stayed in a place, often for a long time, as a resident rather than a visitor.
Hate peace
Prefer quarrels and division, resisting reconciliation even when it is offered.
verses.reflect: What surroundings are wearing you down right now? Tell God honestly how tired you are.
verses.alt: A weary traveler sitting on a low wall at the edge of a crowded village.

verses.title: For peace, met with war
verses.heading: I am in favor of peace
verses.meaning: 'I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war.' The Hebrew says simply, 'I am peace.' Peace is who the singer wants to be. Yet every time he opens his mouth to make peace, others reach for a fight. This ending is unresolved on purpose. The pilgrim leaves this place and starts walking toward Jerusalem, the city whose name sounds like peace, carrying his longing with him.
verses.context: Jerusalem's name is often linked to shalom, peace, and Psalm 122:6 will soon pray for its peace. Jesus said in Matthew 5:9 that peacemakers are blessed and will be called sons of God.
explore: Peace (shalom)
Wholeness and well-being in every relationship, not only the absence of fighting.
Peacemaker
Someone who actively works to reconcile people and end conflict, as Jesus described in Matthew 5:9.
verses.reflect: How can you keep choosing peace even when others choose conflict?
verses.alt: A traveler setting out on a winding road toward distant hills at morning.
